stagnate

/STAG-nayt/ - the stress falls on STAG · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Stagnate means to stop developing, moving, or flowing.

Cut off from the river by the new causeway, the lagoon began to stagnate, its water browning under a skin of algae by July.

Example

The roster stagnated under the cautious new owner — no trades, no signings, no call-ups — until fans could recite the same starting eleven four seasons running.

Stagnate began at the pond's edge: standing water goes foul, and the verb carries that smell wherever it travels. Careers, talks, and towns that stagnate are not merely resting — they are starting to spoil for want of movement.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

languish: To languish is to weaken and fade because nobody tends to you — prisoners languish, unread proposals languish — and real suffering or decay is part of the picture. Something can stagnate in plain sight, fussed over constantly, simply because nothing about it moves or changes.

idle: To idle is to sit unused or tick over without purpose, the way a parked engine idles, and it implies no damage at all — an idle machine is fine. Stagnate always adds spoilage: what stagnates is not resting but starting to go stale from the standstill.

tread water: To tread water is to work steadily just to hold your position — effort in, no ground gained — and the phrase carries no smell of rot. Stagnate is what happens when even that effort stops mattering: the standing still itself begins to sour whatever is standing.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

flourish: to grow vigorously and well

thrive: to do better and better, gaining strength

Where it sits · how much harm the standstill breeds — stall → stagnate → fester

stall vs. stagnate: Stall is milder than stagnate — a stalled project has merely stopped for now, while a stagnating one has begun to sour from standing still.

fester vs. stagnate: Fester is stronger than stagnate — stagnating water has gone still and stale, but a festering problem is actively rotting and getting worse.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — stagn-

Root — stagn-: a pool of standing water (Latin stagnum)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: to be or become

Put it together

Put it together: Stagn- (a pool of standing water, Latin stagnum) + -ate (to become) = to become standing water. Latin stagnare described water with nowhere to go; English kept the literal pond and added everything pond-like — careers, economies, and conversations that sit still long enough to grow a film.

Use the root in a new word: stagnant

Use the root in a new word: stagnant: The stagnant air in the basement had not moved since the last window was painted shut.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / mildly disapproving

Stagnate always disapproves: what stagnates is going stale, not resting. Use it for economies, careers, talks, and ponds; if the pause is healthy or temporary, stall — or plateau, a word you will meet in this unit's reading — is the fairer choice.
